q: Allowed times in a shop are fixed at the level of a perfect performance, with no allowance for ordinary contingencies. As a result, practically every worker shows an adverse variance and earns no bonus, and the incentive scheme loses its effect. The defect in the standard-setting is that:

options.A: The standards were not fixed by work study
options.B: The workers should have been paid at piece rates instead of under a premium bonus scheme
options.C: The standard times should have been revised every month
options.D: Standards fixed for control and incentive purposes should be attainable under normal efficient working, and not set at an ideal level of perfection

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Under the unit-exchange system, a defective assembly removed from a unit under overhaul is replaced at once by a serviced spare assembly, so that the unit is not detained for the repair of its own assembly.
2. The assembly so removed is scrapped forthwith and plays no further part in the system.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 2 only
options.B: Both 1 and 2
options.C: Neither 1 nor 2
options.D: 1 only

q: A clutch in a machine drive differs from a coupling in that a clutch:

options.A: Joins two shafts permanently and cannot be disengaged while running
options.B: Can engage or disengage the transmission of power between the driving and the driven shaft at will, while a coupling makes a permanent connection
options.C: Is used only in belt drives
options.D: Transmits power only through the friction of a belt

q: A flywheel fitted to a workshop machine with a reciprocating or intermittent action, such as a steam engine or a power press, serves mainly to:

options.A: Increase the maximum speed of the machine
options.B: Act as a safety device which breaks under overload
options.C: Store energy during the part of the cycle when the supply exceeds the demand and give it out when the demand exceeds the supply, thus keeping the speed steady
options.D: Convert rotary motion into reciprocating motion

q: In a foundry, the total weight of metal charged in a period is the same as the standard weight for the outturn, but a costlier grade of metal forms a larger proportion of the charge than the standard proportion. The resulting variance in material cost is a:

options.A: Material mix variance
options.B: Material price variance
options.C: Material usage variance
options.D: Yield variance

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. An article which deviates slightly from the prescribed specification may be accepted under a concession (deviation permit) if it is assessed to be fit for its intended use.
2. Acceptance of such a deviating article requires no approval of a competent authority and no record need be kept of it.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 2 only
options.B: Neither 1 nor 2
options.C: 1 only
options.D: Both 1 and 2

q: The quick-return mechanism fitted to a shaping machine ensures that:

options.A: The tool returns to its starting point at the end of the day
options.B: The workpiece is fed back automatically after every cut
options.C: The return stroke of the ram, on which no cutting takes place, is completed in less time than the cutting stroke
options.D: The machine stops automatically at the end of the cut

q: A torque wrench is used by a fitter in a workshop in order to:

options.A: Loosen nuts which have rusted fast
options.B: Measure the diameter of a bolt
options.C: Cut an external thread on a bolt
options.D: Tighten a nut or bolt to a specified tightness (torque), neither under-tight nor over-tight

q: Fitters in a shop repeatedly suffer strain and fatigue because heavy components have to be lifted and held in position by hand throughout an operation. Redesigning the job with lifting tackle and holding fixtures, so that the work is fitted to the capabilities of the worker, is an application of:

options.A: Value analysis
options.B: Work sampling
options.C: Ergonomics
options.D: Job evaluation

q: During the installation of a machine in a workshop, a spirit (bubble) level is used mainly for:

options.A: Measuring the length of the machine bed
options.B: Checking that the bed and guideways of the machine are truly level and in correct alignment, on which the accuracy of the machine depends
options.C: Finding the centre of a round bar
options.D: Testing the insulation of the motor of the machine

q: Under activity-based costing, as applied to the overheads of a workshop, the indirect costs of the workshop are assigned to jobs mainly by:

options.A: Tracing them to the activities performed and assigning them through the cost drivers of those activities
options.B: Dividing them equally among all the jobs executed during the period
options.C: Charging them in proportion to the material cost of each job in every case
options.D: Adding them as a flat percentage of the sale value of the outturn

q: A pyrometer is used in the foundry and heat treatment shops of a workshop in order to:

options.A: Measure the hardness of a casting after it has cooled
options.B: Measure the rotational speed of a furnace blower
options.C: Measure high temperatures, such as those of a furnace or of molten metal
options.D: Measure the pressure developed inside a mould during pouring

q: In life-cycle costing of a workshop machine, the cost considered over the whole life of the machine comprises:

options.A: Only the purchase price paid for the machine at the time of its acquisition
options.B: The acquisition cost together with the operating, maintenance and disposal costs over its life
options.C: Only the maintenance cost incurred after the machine is installed
options.D: Only the depreciation charged on the machine in its first period of use

q: A centre drill used in a workshop is a combined drill and countersink employed mainly for:

options.A: Enlarging a drilled hole to a precise finished size
options.B: Cutting an internal screw thread in a hole
options.C: Removing the burr left at the edge of a drilled hole
options.D: Drilling centre holes in the ends of a workpiece so that it can be held between lathe centres

q: Under FSN analysis, as applied to the material held for workshop use, the items are classified according to:

options.A: The speed at which they move or are consumed, as fast-moving, slow-moving or non-moving items
options.B: The value of each item held in stock
options.C: The country from which each item was procured
options.D: The size and weight of each item in the stock

q: Resilience of a material means the property by which it:

options.A: Can be drawn out into thin wires without breaking
options.B: Continues to deform slowly under a sustained load at high temperature
options.C: Resists indentation and scratching of its surface
options.D: Absorbs energy within its elastic limit and gives it back on removal of the load

q: An angle plate used in the fitting and machine shops of a workshop is a device which serves mainly to:

options.A: Guide a cutting tool along a straight path during an operation
options.B: Measure the angle at which a tool is ground
options.C: Hold and support work truly at a right angle to a machine table or surface plate during marking out or machining
options.D: Check the flatness of a surface by comparison with a standard

q: Under target costing, the allowable cost of a component to be manufactured is arrived at by:

options.A: Adding a desired margin to the cost actually incurred on the component
options.B: Deducting the desired margin from the price at which the component is expected to be acceptable
options.C: Taking the cost of the same component in the previous period, without change
options.D: Averaging the costs quoted by different shops for the component

q: Thread rolling, as carried out for producing external threads in a workshop, is a process in which the threads are:

options.A: Cut by a single-point tool on a lathe, removing metal as chips
options.B: Ground by an abrasive wheel after the blank has been hardened
options.C: Cast along with the blank in a mould prepared for the purpose
options.D: Formed by pressing and rolling dies over the blank, without removing any metal

q: In planning the material required for the Periodic Overhaul programme of a workshop, the procurement lead time of an item means:

options.A: The interval between the placing of the demand or order for the item and its receipt for use
options.B: The time taken by a worker to fit the item on the stock under overhaul
options.C: The period for which the item remains in stock after it is received
options.D: The interval between two successive overhauls of the stock on which the item is used

q: A ball-pein hammer used by fitters and smiths in a workshop is distinguished by the fact that:

options.A: Its head is made of raw hide so that it leaves no mark on the work
options.B: One end of its head is rounded, which is used for riveting and for shaping metal
options.C: Both ends of its head are flat and it is used only for driving chisels
options.D: Its head is split so that it can also be used for drawing out nails

q: A manufacturing account prepared for a workshop for a period is intended mainly to ascertain:

options.A: The profit earned by the workshop on the work done for outside parties
options.B: The amount outstanding against other railways at the close of the period
options.C: The wages payable to the staff of the workshop for the period
options.D: The cost of production of the outturn completed during the period

q: A collet, as used for holding work or tools in a workshop machine, is:

options.A: A split and tapered sleeve which grips a bar or tool firmly and truly concentrically when drawn into its seat
options.B: A flat plate provided with slots for clamping heavy castings to a table
options.C: A revolving centre which supports the free end of a long workpiece
options.D: A flat strap which fastens a heavy casting to the table of a machine

q: The yield point of a metal such as mild steel is the stage in its loading at which:

options.A: The metal finally breaks into two pieces under the load
options.B: The metal attains the highest load it can bear during the test
options.C: The metal begins to deform permanently in a marked manner without any increase in the load applied
options.D: The metal returns completely to its original shape on removal of the load

q: Kaizen, as a practice followed for improvement in a workshop, stands for:

options.A: A complete redesign of the workshop layout carried out at long intervals
options.B: Improvement obtained by replacing all the old machines of a shop at one time
options.C: Continuous and gradual improvement of work processes, made with the involvement of the staff at all levels
options.D: Inspection of the whole outturn of a shop at the final stage only

q: A radius gauge used in a workshop consists of a set of leaves which are used for:

options.A: Checking the radii of curved profiles, fillets and rounded corners of a workpiece
options.B: Measuring the length of a workpiece along a straight edge
options.C: Checking the pitch of a screw thread cut on a workpiece
options.D: Setting the angle of a cutting tool on a machine

q: Under a just-in-time arrangement for the supply of material to a workshop, the material is arranged to reach the shop:

options.A: In one large lot covering the requirement of a long period, well in advance
options.B: Only after the job for which it is required has been completed
options.C: Through the personal custody of the worker executing the job
options.D: As and when it is actually needed for the work in hand, so that the stock and work-in-progress held are kept low

q: An Acme thread, as used in workshop machines and equipment, is a thread form which is:

options.A: A fine thread used only on precision measuring instruments
options.B: A trapezoidal thread form commonly used for the transmission of power, as on lead screws and vices
options.C: A rounded thread used only on the necks of glass bottles and jars
options.D: A thread cut only on pipes for conveying steam and water

q: Poka-yoke devices fitted or adopted in a workshop process are intended mainly to:

options.A: Speed up the movement of material between the shops of the workshop
options.B: Record the time spent by each worker on the jobs executed by him
options.C: Prevent mistakes from occurring, or detect them at the source itself, so that defective work is not produced
options.D: Reduce the number of inspectors required for the final inspection of outturn

q: A thermocouple used for measuring temperature in a workshop works on the principle that:

options.A: A junction of two dissimilar metals produces a voltage which varies with the temperature of the junction
options.B: A column of mercury rises in a glass tube as the temperature rises
options.C: A bimetallic strip bends because its two metals expand at different rates
options.D: The resistance of a coil of wire falls steadily as the temperature rises

q: Codification of the items of material used in a workshop and its stores consists of:

options.A: Arranging the items in the bins of the depot in order of their size
options.B: Recording the name of the supplier against each item in the ledger
options.C: Marking the price of each item on the bin in which it is stocked
options.D: Allotting a systematic code to each item so that it can be identified and accounted for uniformly

q: Gang milling, as carried out on a milling machine in a workshop, consists of:

options.A: Milling a workpiece in several separate passes of a single cutter
options.B: Milling the same surface alternately with two different machines
options.C: Holding several workpieces together and milling them one after the other
options.D: Mounting several cutters on the same arbor so that a number of surfaces are milled in one pass

q: The factor of safety adopted in the design of a machine part is expressed as the ratio of:

options.A: The working load on the part to the load at which it finally fails
options.B: The load at which the part finally fails to the safe working load allowed on it
options.C: The weight of the part to the load carried by it in service
options.D: The cost of the part to the cost of the machine in which it is fitted

q: Simplification, as applied to the components and materials used in a workshop, consists mainly of:

options.A: Laying down the standard specifications to which a component must conform
options.B: Inspecting every component of a batch before it is accepted for use
options.C: Reducing the unnecessary variety of types and sizes of components to the minimum necessary
options.D: Giving a separate code number to every variety of component in use

q: A pilot hole drilled in a workpiece in a workshop is:

options.A: A small hole drilled in advance to guide the larger drill which finally enlarges it to the required size
options.B: A hole drilled through a jig bush only for the purpose of testing the jig
options.C: A hole left unfinished in a component for inspection by the accounts office
options.D: A hole drilled in scrap material for trying out a new drill

q: The machinability of a metal, as the term is used in a machine shop, refers to:

options.A: The ease with which the metal can be cast into the required shape
options.B: The ease with which the metal can be welded to other metals
options.C: The resistance offered by the metal to corrosion in service
options.D: The ease with which the metal can be machined, judged by tool life, surface finish and the power required

q: Grouting carried out during the installation of a machine in a workshop consists of:

options.A: Filling the space under the base of the machine with cement grout so that it is secured truly and its load is distributed over the foundation
options.B: Applying a thick coat of paint to the foundation to protect it from oil
options.C: Packing the bearings of the machine with grease before it is started
options.D: Levelling the floor of the shop by laying a fresh layer of concrete over it

q: A wire gauge used in a workshop is an instrument employed for measuring:

options.A: The length of wire required for winding the armature of a motor
options.B: The electrical resistance of a length of wire in a circuit
options.C: The thickness of sheet metal and the diameter of wires, by trying them in its graded slots
options.D: The tension at which a wire rope of a crane is working

q: In the Charpy impact test carried out on a specimen of material in a workshop, the property assessed is found from:

options.A: The load required to pull the specimen apart in a testing machine
options.B: The depth of the impression made on the specimen by a hardened ball
options.C: The energy absorbed by a notched specimen when it is broken by a swinging pendulum
options.D: The number of twists the specimen bears before it finally fails

q: Lagging provided on the boilers and steam pipes of a workshop consists of:

options.A: A covering of heat-insulating material, applied to reduce the loss of heat from the surface
options.B: A layer of metal sheet applied to strengthen the shell of the boiler
options.C: A coat of red lead applied to prevent rusting of the pipes
options.D: A jacket through which cold water is circulated to cool the pipes

q: End milling, as carried out in a workshop, is the operation of producing:

options.A: Flat surfaces only, with the flat face of a large cutter
options.B: Slots, pockets and profiled shapes with a cutter which cuts on its end as well as on its periphery
options.C: Screw threads on a cylindrical workpiece with a rotating cutter
options.D: Gear teeth on a blank by a generating process

q: Backlash in the mating parts of a machine, such as gear teeth or a screw and nut, means:

options.A: The extra load thrown on the parts when the machine is suddenly stopped
options.B: The wear which takes place on the parts after long use in service
options.C: The heating of the parts when the machine is run at high speed
options.D: The play or lost motion between the parts, felt when the direction of movement is reversed

q: High-speed steel, widely used for the cutting tools of a workshop, is valued mainly because it:

options.A: Can be easily cast into intricate shapes at a low temperature
options.B: Is lighter in weight than all other steels used in a workshop
options.C: Does not require any grinding or sharpening during its whole life
options.D: Retains its cutting hardness even at the high temperatures reached in fast cutting

q: The safety valve fitted on a boiler in a workshop is a device which:

options.A: Regulates the supply of feed water to the boiler during its working
options.B: Indicates the level of water standing inside the boiler at any time
options.C: Opens automatically and lets out steam when the pressure in the boiler rises beyond the safe limit
options.D: Removes the sediment collected at the bottom of the boiler during working

q: A universal bevel protractor used in a workshop is an instrument employed for:

options.A: Measuring and checking angles accurately, with the help of its graduated scale and vernier
options.B: Marking lines parallel to the edge of a workpiece on a surface plate
options.C: Checking whether a surface is truly flat and level
options.D: Measuring the depth of a hole or recess in a workpiece

q: Chatter occurring during a machining operation in a workshop refers to:

options.A: The noise made by workers while a machine is in operation
options.B: The vibration set up between the cutting tool and the work, which leaves marks and spoils the finish of the surface
options.C: The breaking of the cutting tool when it meets a hard spot in the work
options.D: The rattling of loose material kept on the table of the machine

q: In a crucible furnace used in a workshop foundry, the metal is melted:

options.A: In direct contact with the fuel in a tall shaft furnace
options.B: In a rotating drum in which the metal is tumbled with the fuel
options.C: On an open hearth over which a flame is played by a burner
options.D: In a container, the crucible, which is heated from outside and from which the molten metal is poured

q: Metallography, as carried out for the examination of metals in a workshop, consists of:

options.A: Testing a specimen to destruction in a machine to find its strength
options.B: Examining the polished and etched surface of a specimen under a microscope to study its grain and structure
options.C: Analysing a specimen chemically to find the proportion of each element in it
options.D: Photographing a casting with rays to reveal the defects inside it

q: Parting sand used in making a foundry mould in a workshop is the dry sand which is sprinkled on the joint face of the mould in order to:

options.A: Give a smooth finish to the surface of the casting produced
options.B: Increase the strength of the mould so that it bears the weight of the metal
options.C: Allow the gases formed during pouring to escape from the mould
options.D: Prevent the two halves of the mould from sticking together, so that they can be separated

q: The depth of cut in a machining operation in a workshop means:

options.A: The thickness of the layer of metal removed from the workpiece in one pass of the tool
options.B: The distance travelled by the tool along the work in one revolution
options.C: The speed at which the cutting edge of the tool moves over the work
options.D: The total depth to which a hole is drilled in a workpiece

q: Parallax error in reading a measuring instrument in a workshop arises when:

options.A: The instrument has not been set to zero before the measurement is taken
options.B: The scale of the instrument has worn out and cannot be read clearly
options.C: The reading is observed from an oblique position instead of squarely in line with the pointer or graduation
options.D: The workpiece expands on account of the heat generated during machining

q: Metallising (metal spraying), as used for reclamation work in a workshop, is a process in which a worn part such as a shaft is built up by:

options.A: Welding a sleeve of new metal over the whole length of the part
options.B: Spraying molten metal on to its prepared surface, and machining it back to size afterwards
options.C: Electroplating a thick layer of metal on the part in a bath
options.D: Shrinking a heated ring of metal on to the worn portion of the part

q: The fluidity of a molten metal, as the term is used in a workshop foundry, means its ability to:

options.A: Resist oxidation while it remains in the furnace in the molten state
options.B: Solidify quickly as soon as it is poured into the mould
options.C: Flow readily and fill the mould cavity completely before it solidifies
options.D: Retain its heat for a long time after it is poured into the mould

q: Commissioning of a machine newly installed in a workshop means:

options.A: Entering the machine in the Plant Register of the workshop after its purchase
options.B: Sanctioning the estimate for the purchase of the machine by the competent authority
options.C: Testing and trialling the machine after its erection and putting it into regular service
options.D: Despatching the machine from the workshop for repairs at another unit

q: The viscosity of the lubricating oil used in the machines of a workshop refers to:

options.A: The resistance of the oil to flow, which governs its ability to maintain a lubricating film between moving surfaces
options.B: The temperature at which the oil begins to give off inflammable vapour
options.C: The proportion of impurities present in the oil as supplied
options.D: The rate at which the oil is consumed by a machine in service

q: A follower rest (travelling steady) used during the turning of a long and slender shaft differs from a fixed steady rest in that the follower rest:

options.A: Is bolted to the lathe bed at one fixed point and supports the shaft only at that point
options.B: Is mounted on the carriage and travels along the bed with the cutting tool, supporting the shaft close to the point of cut
options.C: Is fitted inside the headstock spindle and rotates with the shaft
options.D: Holds the shaft in a chuck while the tool is fed by hand

q: The dead centre fitted in the tailstock of a centre lathe is so called because:

options.A: It does not rotate with the work, the workpiece turning on the centre itself
options.B: It is made of dead-soft metal which cannot be hardened
options.C: It is used only for holding condemned and unserviceable stock
options.D: It is fitted permanently in the tailstock and can never be removed

q: The carriage of a centre lathe is the assembly which:

options.A: Houses the spindle and the gearing which drives it
options.B: Supports the workpiece from the tailstock end of the lathe
options.C: Slides along the bedways of the lathe and carries the cross slide and the tool post, moving the tool along the work
options.D: Converts the rotary motion of the motor into the reciprocating motion of the tool

q: The compound slide (compound rest) provided on the carriage of a centre lathe serves mainly to allow:

options.A: The workpiece to be rotated at two different speeds at the same time
options.B: The tailstock to be set over for turning long tapers
options.C: The chuck to be tightened without the use of a key
options.D: The cutting tool to be fed at an angle to the axis of the lathe, as required for turning short tapers and chamfers

q: In climb (down) milling, the distinguishing feature of the operation is that:

options.A: The cutter rotates so that its teeth at the point of contact move in the same direction as the feed of the work
options.B: The cutter rotates against the direction of the feed of the work throughout the cut
options.C: The work is fed upwards against a stationary cutter
options.D: Several cutters are mounted together on the same arbor for the operation

q: Face milling, as carried out on a milling machine in a workshop, is the operation of:

options.A: Cutting a groove of the shape of the cutter in the edge of the workpiece
options.B: Producing a flat surface with a cutter whose axis is at right angles to the surface being machined
options.C: Generating the teeth of a gear on a gear blank
options.D: Enlarging a drilled hole to an accurate size and finish

q: The helical flutes formed along the body of a twist drill serve mainly to:

options.A: Reduce the weight of the drill so that it can be held by hand
options.B: Mark the size of the drill on its body for identification
options.C: Form the cutting edges of the drill and provide a passage by which the chips escape and the cutting fluid reaches the cutting edges
options.D: Prevent the drill from being used in a drilling machine

q: A bench drilling machine of the sensitive type is preferred for drilling small holes in workshop work mainly because:

options.A: Its spindle is driven at a fixed speed which cannot be altered
options.B: It drills holes without the workpiece being held or clamped
options.C: It is worked without any cutting fluid on all materials
options.D: The feed is applied by a hand lever, so that the operator can feel the progress of the drill and avoid breaking the small drill

q: A grinding wheel in use in a workshop is said to be glazed when:

options.A: Its face has become smooth and shiny because the abrasive grains have dulled without breaking away, so that the wheel ceases to cut properly
options.B: Its abrasive grains have been coated with oil by the operator before use
options.C: It has been purposely made with a mirror finish for polishing work
options.D: It has cracked across its face and has become unfit for use

q: A surface grinder installed in a workshop is used mainly for:

options.A: Cutting external screw threads on shafts and bolts
options.B: Melting and pouring metal into moulds for castings
options.C: Producing flat surfaces to a high degree of flatness and surface finish, the work being commonly held on a magnetic chuck
options.D: Drilling deep holes in long shafts from one end

q: A jenny caliper (odd-leg caliper) is used by a fitter in marking out work mainly for:

options.A: Measuring the internal diameter of a bore directly from its scale
options.B: Checking the pitch of a screw thread cut on a shaft
options.C: Measuring the thickness of a plate at a point far from its edge
options.D: Scribing a line parallel to an edge of the workpiece, one leg riding on the edge while the pointed leg marks the line, and for locating the centre of a round bar

q: A scriber, as used in the fitting shop of a workshop, is an instrument employed for:

options.A: Making a deep indentation at the centre point of a hole to be drilled
options.B: Scratching fine layout lines on the surface of the metal to mark out the work before machining or fitting
options.C: Measuring the depth of a hole or recess in a component
options.D: Checking whether a machined surface is truly flat and level

q: A vernier height gauge is used on a surface plate in a workshop mainly for:

options.A: Measuring heights of workpieces accurately and scribing lines on work at a set height during marking out
options.B: Holding a workpiece firmly while it is being filed by hand
options.C: Testing the hardness of a component at different heights
options.D: Supporting a long shaft at the correct height for turning

q: A combination set, as used in marking out and fitting work in a workshop, consists of:

options.A: A set of drills of assorted sizes kept in one box
options.B: A set of taps used one after another for cutting an internal thread
options.C: A steel rule used with interchangeable heads, such as a square head, a protractor head and a centre head, for laying out work, checking angles and finding the centre of round stock
options.D: A set of files of different cuts used for finishing a surface

q: A plumb bob is used in the erection and fitting work of a workshop for:

options.A: Measuring the weight of a component suspended from a crane
options.B: Establishing a true vertical line, the pointed weight suspended on a cord aligning itself with the direction of gravity
options.C: Checking the level of a machine bed in the horizontal plane
options.D: Marking a circle of large radius on a plate to be cut

q: In bench work in the fitting shop of a workshop, a component which is to be filed, sawn or chipped by hand is held firmly for the operation in:

options.A: A pair of tongs held by an assistant
options.B: The jaws of a chuck fitted on a lathe
options.C: A moulding flask filled with sand
options.D: A bench vice fitted on the work bench

q: A pin punch is used by a fitter in a workshop mainly for:

options.A: Driving out pins, dowels and similar fastenings from their holes in an assembly
options.B: Marking the centre of a hole before it is drilled
options.C: Cutting a keyway in the bore of a pulley
options.D: Expanding the end of a tube before it is fitted

q: A cross-cut (cape) chisel used in fitting work is distinguished by its narrow cutting edge and is employed mainly for:

options.A: Removing a thick layer of metal from a flat surface in one pass
options.B: Dressing the face of a grinding wheel to restore its cutting action
options.C: Cutting grooves and keyways and cutting channels in metal surfaces
options.D: Shearing thin sheets of metal along a marked line

q: A ring spanner (box-end spanner) differs from an open-ended spanner in that the ring spanner:

options.A: Can be used only on pipes and round fittings
options.B: Grips the nut or bolt head all round, enclosing it, so that it is less likely to slip or damage the corners of the head
options.C: Has an adjustable jaw which can be set to any size of nut
options.D: Is used for driving screws with a hexagonal recess in the head

q: An Allen key (hex key) is the tool used in a workshop for:

options.A: Gripping and turning water pipes and pipe fittings
options.B: Measuring the clearance between two mating surfaces
options.C: Striking light blows on a chisel while cutting metal
options.D: Tightening and loosening socket-head screws which have a hexagonal recess in the head

q: A pipe wrench, as used by fitters in a workshop, is a tool designed mainly for:

options.A: Gripping and turning round pipes and pipe fittings, its serrated jaws biting into the pipe as the handle is pulled
options.B: Cutting a pipe to the required length at the work bench
options.C: Cutting an external thread on the end of a pipe
options.D: Measuring the bore of a pipe before it is fitted

q: Tin snips are used in the sheet-metal work of a workshop for:

options.A: Bending a thick plate to a right angle in one operation
options.B: Punching holes of a fixed size in a metal sheet
options.C: Cutting thin metal sheets by hand along straight or curved lines
options.D: Joining two sheets together by folding their edges in a press

q: Fullering, as carried out in forging work in the smithy of a workshop, consists of:

options.A: Joining two pieces of heated metal together by hammering them at welding heat
options.B: Pressing a fuller into the heated work to form a neck or groove at a place, from which the metal is then drawn out
options.C: Hardening the finished work by heating it and cooling it suddenly in water
options.D: Piercing a hole through a heated bar with a punch and a hammer

q: Swaging, as carried out in the smithy of a workshop, consists of:

options.A: Cutting a heated bar into pieces of the required length
options.B: Coating a forged article with a protective layer of another metal
options.C: Melting scrap metal in a furnace for making fresh castings
options.D: Shaping and finishing a workpiece to a round or other regular section by working it between swages, which act as dies

q: The anvil provided in the smithy of a workshop is used for:

options.A: Supporting the heated workpiece while it is hammered and forged into shape
options.B: Storing the hand tools of the smith when they are not in use
options.C: Melting small quantities of metal for repairs to castings
options.D: Holding a workpiece firmly for filing and fitting operations

q: A sledge hammer is provided in a workshop for work of the kind in which:

options.A: Very light taps are required on delicate measuring instruments
options.B: A screw has to be driven into a threaded hole by turning
options.C: Heavy striking blows are required, as in heavy forging and driving work, the hammer being swung with both hands
options.D: A surface has to be scraped flat by hand to a fine finish

q: A power hammer installed in the smithy of a workshop is a machine which:

options.A: Cuts metal bars to length by the repeated blows of a blade
options.B: Delivers repeated forging blows by mechanical power, enabling heavy sections to be forged which cannot be worked by hand hammering
options.C: Presses bearings into their housings without any blow or impact
options.D: Rotates a workpiece while a tool is pressed against it by hand

q: In a workshop foundry, the molten metal is carried from the furnace to the moulds for pouring in:

options.A: A moulding flask lined with green sand
options.B: A wooden box fitted with handles at both ends
options.C: A wheelbarrow kept specially for foundry work
options.D: A ladle, which is a refractory-lined vessel provided for holding and pouring the molten metal

q: An oxidising flame in oxy-acetylene welding is a flame in which:

options.A: Oxygen is present in excess of the acetylene, the flame tending to burn and oxidise the metal being welded
options.B: Acetylene is present in large excess of the oxygen supplied
options.C: Oxygen and acetylene are supplied in exactly equal proportions
options.D: No oxygen from a cylinder is used and air alone supports the flame

q: A flashback, as the term is used in gas welding in a workshop, is the dangerous occurrence in which:

options.A: The flame goes out with a snap because the gas supply is exhausted
options.B: A shower of sparks is thrown out from the weld as the metal melts
options.C: The flame travels back through the blowpipe and into the hose towards the gas supply, with risk of explosion
options.D: The welded joint cracks along its length as it cools after welding

q: Slag inclusion, as a defect found in a welded joint in a workshop, means that:

options.A: The weld metal has flowed over the surface of the joint without fusing with it
options.B: Particles of slag have remained trapped inside the weld metal instead of floating out of it, weakening the joint
options.C: The joint has been left with a hollow groove along the edge of the weld
options.D: The parent metal has melted away excessively below the joint

q: Lack of fusion, as a defect in a welded joint made in a workshop, means that:

options.A: The weld metal contains a large number of small gas cavities throughout it
options.B: The finished weld stands too high above the surface of the parent metal
options.C: The joint has become distorted and out of shape on cooling after welding
options.D: The weld metal has not properly united with the parent metal or with an earlier run of weld, leaving unjoined surfaces within the joint

q: Wrought iron, as a material handled in a workshop, is distinguished in that it is:

options.A: A very pure form of iron of low carbon content, having a fibrous structure due to slag contained in it, and is readily forged and welded
options.B: An alloy of iron containing a high proportion of carbon, cast into moulds for machine parts
options.C: A steel containing chromium, used mainly for parts which must not rust
options.D: A mixture of copper and tin used for casting bearings and bushes

q: Brass, widely used in a workshop for fittings and components, is an alloy consisting essentially of:

options.A: Copper and tin in roughly equal proportions
options.B: Iron and carbon with a small proportion of manganese
options.C: Copper and zinc
options.D: Aluminium and copper with magnesium

q: Bronze, used in a workshop for bushes, bearings and similar components, is an alloy consisting essentially of:

options.A: Copper and zinc
options.B: Copper and tin
options.C: Lead and tin
options.D: Iron and nickel

q: Pig iron, as the term is used in connection with workshop foundries and materials, is:

options.A: The finished casting taken out of a mould after it has cooled
options.B: The scrap iron collected from the shops for disposal as waste
options.C: A refined and pure form of iron ready for use in precision instruments
options.D: The iron obtained directly from the smelting of iron ore in a blast furnace, an impure and high-carbon material from which cast iron, steel and wrought iron are made

q: White metal (Babbitt metal), used in the workshops for lining and re-metalling bearings, is:

options.A: A soft tin-based alloy which provides a low-friction bearing surface against a steel shaft
options.B: A hard steel alloyed with tungsten for making cutting tools
options.C: A coating of zinc applied on iron sheets to protect them from rust
options.D: A pure form of aluminium used for casting light components

q: In the extrusion process of forming metal, as applied to the production of sections and rods, the metal is shaped by:

options.A: Hammering a heated billet repeatedly until it takes the shape of a die
options.B: Pouring the molten metal into a mould of the required section
options.C: Forcing the heated metal through an opening in a die of the required cross-section, so that it emerges as a long length of that section
options.D: Rolling a flat plate into a tube and welding the joint along its length

q: Wire is produced from metal rods by the drawing process, in which:

options.A: The rod is melted and the liquid metal is allowed to fall in a thin stream
options.B: The rod is pulled through dies of successively smaller opening, reducing its diameter and increasing its length
options.C: The rod is twisted rapidly until it stretches into a thin wire
options.D: The rod is cut into thin strips which are then rolled into wire

q: Metal spinning, as carried out in a workshop, is the process of forming:

options.A: Screw threads on the outside of a rod by rotating it under a die
options.B: Long wires by pulling a rod through a series of dies
options.C: Metal sheets into tubes by rolling and joining the edges
options.D: Hollow circular articles from a rotating sheet-metal blank by pressing the blank, as it spins, over a former on a lathe-type machine

q: A split pin is used with a bolt and nut in workshop assemblies mainly in order to:

options.A: Lock the nut against slackening back, the pin passing through a hole in the bolt beyond the nut and its ends being bent over
options.B: Fill the clearance between the bolt and the hole in which it fits
options.C: Increase the clamping force exerted by the nut on the joint
options.D: Prevent the bolt from rusting at the threaded portion

q: A circlip, as used in the assembly of machine parts in a workshop, is a fastener which:

options.A: Is hammered into a drilled hole to join two plates permanently
options.B: Is screwed into one part to bear upon another and prevent its movement
options.C: Springs into a groove on a shaft or in a bore and thereby retains a component in position on the shaft or in the bore
options.D: Is wrapped round a joint to make it leak-proof against steam and water

q: A grub screw (set screw), as used in workshop assemblies, differs from an ordinary bolt in that the grub screw:

options.A: Has a large head which is turned with a spanner from outside the assembly
options.B: Is threaded along its whole length and has no head, being screwed wholly into one part so that its end bears on another part and prevents relative movement between them
options.C: Is always used together with a split pin to lock it in place
options.D: Is made only of soft metal so that it can be cut to length on the spot

q: In a journal (plain) bearing fitted in workshop machinery, the rotating shaft is supported by:

options.A: A set of balls which roll between the shaft and the outer casing of the bearing
options.B: A set of tapered rollers held in a cage inside the bearing housing
options.C: A magnetic field which keeps the shaft suspended without any contact
options.D: Sliding contact between the journal of the shaft and the surface of the bearing bush, the two being separated in running by a film of lubricant

q: The rake angle provided on a single-point cutting tool used in a workshop is the angle of inclination of the face of the tool, and it is provided mainly in order to:

options.A: Allow the chip formed in cutting to flow freely away over the face of the tool, so that the cutting action is eased
options.B: Prevent the underside of the tool from rubbing against the surface already machined
options.C: Strengthen the point of the tool against breaking under the cut
options.D: Fix the height at which the tool is set in the tool post of the machine
